title: Restless in Sleepy Hollow
author: https://hedgehogreview.com/contributors/nick-burns
text:
Years ago, on one of those perfect, blade-sharp November days, I paid a visit to the village of Sleepy Hollow with my then girlfriend. We toured a seventeenth-century mill and strolled through the cemetery and past the Old Dutch Church as the short afternoon ended, falling leaves dark against the red light.

The village seemed so romantically frozen in the past that we could easily imagine old Colonial ghosts stealing along the side paths and across the bridge just short of where, in Washington Irving’s famous story, the schoolteacher Ichabod Crane was felled by a missile hurled by his headless pursuer. The Manhattan skyline was just visible from the top of the cemetery hill, but the churn of the city felt nowhere near.

That sense of the place as a shelter from the restlessness of a nation on the move was, as it turns out, Irving’s motive for choosing the village as the setting for his “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow,” as his narrator explains in the story itself:

Local tales and superstitions thrive best in these sheltered long-settled retreats; but are trampled underfoot by the shifting throng that forms the population of most of our country places. Besides, there is no encouragement for ghosts in most of our villages, for they have scarcely had time to finish their first nap, and turn themselves in their graves, before their surviving friends have travelled away from the neighborhood; so that when they turn out at night to walk their rounds, they have no acquaintance left to call upon. This is perhaps the reason why we so seldom hear of ghosts except in our long-established Dutch communities.

Reading the story in preparation for the visit, I was struck by the implications of that passage. I had thought of Washington Irving in simple terms, as both the most and least successful American writer: least, because few American writers are held in greater contempt by the country’s literary critics and English professors; most, because no other American writer has managed to meld his work so seamlessly with our national mythology. It is not necessary to actually read “Rip Van Winkle” or “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow” to know the stories: For children, the figure of the headless rider with a pumpkin at his side is simply part of the ubiquitous imagery of Halloween, their favorite holiday.

And walking through Sleepy Hollow two hundred years after those tales first appeared, I found that Irving remains the hero of that town. Headless Horseman–themed decorations festoon the lopsided, off-white clapboard houses, the shop windows, and firehouses. In a jazz bar down an alley, a bartender told us that homecoming football games always feature a halftime ride by the famous beheaded equestrian. What American writer has enjoyed such lasting fame off the back of a single short story?

So I was delighted to learn of a new book on Irving by Phillip Lopate, whose excellent anthology, Writing New York, was an invaluable aide in my effort to immerse myself in the deep history of the city during the five years I lived there. New Yorkers, I had discovered, are nostalgists for the metropolis of yesterday, the “vanishing New York” of pre-Giuliani grittiness and cultural ferment, but they seem to have little interest in the city’s deep past—the Dutch era, Colonial times, or even the nineteenth century. Such antiquarianism, they seem to think, is for lesser cities such as Chicago, whose residents still talk about the 1893 World’s Fair as though it took place only yesterday. By the time New York ghosts finish their first nap, the city has moved on to something else. Such is life in a city whose oldest tradition is endless, merciless transformation. Watching that process grind on in a million small ways—the shuttering of a beloved bar, the gentrifying of a neighborhood—always filled me with horror.

I wanted to learn about New York’s deep past precisely to throw a wrench into the gears of change, and Lopate’s lovingly assembled collection was perfectly fit for that purpose. Recommendations for the cheap eateries of the early nineteenth century (don’t order a drink; just enjoy a “tumbler of cool Croton,” as tap water from the new aquifer was called), an honest love story of the East Village by Willa Cather, Mayakovsky’s unequaled ode to the Brooklyn Bridge: Here was evidence that not everything could be trampled by the “shifting throng.”

Washington Irving (1783–1859), a native son of New York City, provided further assistance. His first work, the History of New York (1809), written under the guise of old Dutch curmudgeon Diedrich Knickerbocker, was a satirical but genuine lament over the city’s infidelity to its past. But as the passage from “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow” attests, he soon learned that such faithlessness was not confined to the metropolis on the Hudson.

American restlessness proved to be a literary challenge as well as an emotional one. On one level, Irving was joking when he said that ghost stories are scarce in America because the ghosts scarcely have a chance to settle in their graves before their descendants leave for better prospects in the Ohio country. But beneath his levity is a sincere awareness of the American social landscape’s hostility to literature. The folk traditions that so often supply writers with raw material simply have too little time to settle in and gain purchase in a country so bent on change as our own. Little wonder that Southern literature has such an exceptional place in American literary history, given the region’s historically static social world and agrarian economy. Little wonder, too, that Irving himself soon decamped for England and Spain, where there were richer veins of ghost stories for him to mine than in the long-extinguished New Netherland colony.

Lopate notes that Irving faced criticism—including from James Fenimore Cooper—that he worked too hard to impress European (and especially British) audiences, betraying his own country in the process. Irving’s major biographer, Stanley T. Williams, considered him responsible for a “cult of elegance” that prevented American literature from becoming truly American until the Civil War. One might respond that Irving’s efforts to woo European audiences put American literature on the map, silencing the jeers of Englishmen such as Sydney Smith (1771–1845), who asked, “Who reads an American book?”

But Irving merits a more aggressive defense from such accusations. Beneath his apparently light literature lies a subtle and fully American dissent against America: the revulsion of a native son for the cultural and human impoverishment generated by the nation’s unthinking devotion to movement, change, and disruption. He went to Europe because it was old and he could no longer bear America’s newness.

But he could not escape the American predicament. Evocative as were his descriptions of the decaying Alhambra, he could never stand in relation to it in the way a Spaniard could: It represented connections to a mythic past that was not, and never could be, his own. Nor was Europe free of the modern dislocations that were only more advanced in America. Returning to Spain as American ambassador amid the political struggles of the mid-1800s, Irving, Lopate reports, found Madrid no longer charming.

Returning to America, he sought to build a quiet writer’s retreat at Sunnyside, just down the Hudson from Sleepy Hollow. But his country, which took no rest itself, would allow him none: A railway company soon broke ground just below his house, and the incessant noise of the trains would prove a distraction to his work. Such details make Lopate’s impressionistic biography a bit like certain works by its subject: slight, but thoroughly entertaining. And as in his superb anthology of New York writing, Lopate excels in his artful selection of excerpts and quotes.

To be a writer in America is to cut against the grain. Irving’s awareness of this fact is enough for us to judge him a fitting figure to stand at the headwaters of the national literature—enough not to feel ashamed of him, even if he was, in many regards, as Lopate acknowledges, a minor writer, often a hack writer, who wrote many bad books and possessed only a small fraction of the talent of Poe, Hawthorne, or Melville. The success of his tales, among the American people if not among the literary critics and professors, attests to their effectiveness as antidotes to the dearth of mythology that their author sensed and deplored in his own land.

But they are also myths in the sense of lies—comforting untruths that we continue to tell ourselves in spite of all the evidence to the contrary. What historical research I have done into the area around Sleepy Hollow suggests that its inhabitants were scattered and often desperate tenant farmers on a large land grant, closer to European peasants than the happy Dutch yeomen of Irving’s tale, and, because they were ethnically diverse, they did not enjoy the collective cultural comforts of Old World serfdom.

I myself fell under the spell of Irving’s lies on my visit to Sleepy Hollow, by imagining the village much as he did, as a comforting and unchanging haven tucked away from the chaos and impermanence of the metropolis. As I later discovered, Sleepy Hollow is a fiction, even down to the name itself.

Until 1996, this part of Westchester County was called “North Tarrytown,” a name chosen in the late nineteenth century for a reason that indicates its inhabitants were not free from the imperatives of change facing the rest of the nation: Tarrytown, to the south, was a budding industrial center, and their neighbors to the north thought they might be able to capitalize on its success by adopting a modified version of the name.

By the middle of the twentieth century, North Tarrytown’s efforts to draw industry had succeeded brilliantly: A huge General Motors plant anchored the local economy and drew emigrants from as far away as French Canada, Poland, and Slovakia, submerging whatever vestiges remained of the area’s Dutch character. But that plant closed, like so many others up and down the Hudson River, when the area deindustrialized in the postwar decades, an experience from which many of its towns have yet to recover.

“Sleepy Hollow” was an exercise in “rebranding,” as the village looked to tourism to help its shattered economy, taking advantage of the fact that the dramatic conclusion of Irving’s famous story takes place within its boundaries. Today, the village hardly resembles the one that Irving described as a place whose inhabitants stay put from generation to generation. Instead, it exemplifies the demographic transformations that, even more than in Irving’s time, characterize the country as a whole. Ecuadorians and people from other Latin American countries began to arrive in the last days of the GM plant and now make up more than half of the village’s population, reversing its population decline.

Walking back toward the station to wait for the train that would carry us past Irving’s Sunnyside and back to the city, we passed through the small downtown, most of its shops bearing names at least half in Spanish: La Famosa Mini Market, Peluquería Original. The bartender who had told us about the ride of the Headless Horseman at the homecoming football games was herself the child of Ecuadorian immigrants. I should have asked her what she thought about that tradition. It must be strange to have your civic identity tied to a story about a village whose population is quintessentially rooted and unchanging—a village that obviously bears little resemblance to the real one to which your parents moved from another continent, in the process uprooting themselves from the traditions of that place.

Every well-told lie has room for many things—even, perhaps, the truth. Characteristically, Irving’s story does testify to the American displacement it seems to put to one side. Ichabod Crane, its protagonist, is an interloper, an itinerant schoolteacher, and the story ends with his banishment, his rival for the affections of a local farm girl having driven him away in the disguise of the Headless Horseman. Smote by a pumpkin, Crane vanishes without a trace and is quickly replaced by another itinerant schoolteacher. Given the history of America, such a fate is spooky indeed.
